concerns.text: FR-006 mandates using the Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) with a t-distribution for cross-snapshot variance. This is statistically invalid for turbulence data. Turbulent fields exhibit strong spatial correlation (integral scales) and temporal correlation. Treating 3-5 snapshots as independent samples for a t-test on derived statistics (like bias at a specific wavenumber) ignores the effective degrees of freedom. The variance of the mean of correlated fields does not scale as 1/N. This method will produce artificially narrow confidence intervals, leading to false positives in significance testing. A block-bootstrap or effective sample size correction is required.

SC-002 and US-2 define the 'ground truth' exponent as the 'empirically fitted value from the 1024³ dataset' and measure deviation against it. This creates a circular validation loop for the 'bias' metric. If the 1024³ dataset itself has finite-Reynolds-number deviations (which it does), the 'bias' calculated against it conflates 'resolution error' with 'finite-Re error'. The spec claims to measure 'resolution-induced errors' but validates them against a reference that contains the very errors it seeks to isolate. The validation target is not independent of the predictor's systematic error source.

US-1 Acceptance Scenario 2 requires that 'high-wavenumber modes (k > N_down/2) satisfy a maximum absolute value < 1e-12' after Fourier truncation. While mathematically true for exact arithmetic, in floating-point arithmetic (double precision), spectral truncation followed by inverse FFT and re-FFT (or spatial downsampling) introduces round-off noise. Requiring a hard floor of 1e-12 on the *reconstructed* downsampled field's high modes is physically unrealistic and may cause the system to fail valid runs due to numerical noise, not algorithmic failure. The threshold should be relative to the energy spectrum or machine epsilon, not an absolute float constant.
